context: He has just foretold Dante's exile and charged him to write down everything he has seen.

quote: the bitter mingled with the sweet
note: The bitter is the exile just foretold. The sweet is the promise that his poem will last and do good.

quote: Him who lifts the burden of every wrong
note: God, who sets every injustice right. Beatrice reminds Dante that the wrong done to him will not go unanswered.

quote: Paradise exists not only in my eyes
note: A gentle rebuke. Dante is so lost in her face that he forgets the other souls, who also reflect God's light.
Mars, the fifth of the heavens counting up from the Moon. The souls who appear in it fought for the faith.

quote: the tree that draws life from its crown
note: Paradise pictured as a tree, with the heavens as its tiers of branches. Unlike an earthly tree it is fed from the top, from God, and it is never out of season.
The souls of Mars appear as lights that form a great cross with equal arms, first seen in Canto 14.
The successor of Moses, who led the Israelites into the Promised Land and conquered it. His story is the biblical Book of Joshua.
Judas Maccabeus, who led the Jewish revolt against the Syrian Greek king Antiochus in the 2nd century BC and won back the Temple in Jerusalem. His wars are told in the Books of Maccabees.
A child's spinning top, kept turning by lashing it with a cord. Joy does the lashing here. Virgil uses the same toy in a simile in the Aeneid.

context: Honored here for his wars against the Saracens in Spain, as the French epics told them.

note: William, count of Orange, who fought the Saracens in southern France under Charlemagne and died a monk in 812. He is the hero of a cycle of Old French epic poems.
A character from the same epics: a giant Saracen who is baptized and fights beside William with a huge club. He never existed, but Dante and his age took the poems for history.
Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lower Lorraine, a leader of the First Crusade. When Jerusalem fell in 1099 he became its first Christian ruler, and died the next year.

A Norman adventurer who conquered most of southern Italy in the 11th century, taking it from the Byzantine Greeks and, with his brother, Sicily from the Saracens. He died in 1085. Inferno 28 recalls the dead of his wars.

quote: The soul that had been speaking to me
note: Dante's ancestor goes back to his place in the cross and joins the singing. This is the last we see of him.
They have risen to the next heaven, a larger sphere. As at every ascent, Dante feels no motion. He knows it only because Beatrice has grown more beautiful.
A blush fading from a fair face: the red light of Mars gives way to the white light of Jupiter.

context: Astronomers called Jupiter temperate because it lies between hot Mars and cold Saturn.

quote: now D, now I, now L
note: The first three letters of the Latin sentence spelled out below. The souls form one letter at a time, like writing in the sky.

Dante's Italian calls on a goddess, "diva Pegasea": a Muse. The Muses took the title from the winged horse Pegasus, whose hoof struck open their sacred spring on Mount Helicon. Which Muse is meant is not said.
The Latin sentence has thirty-five letters.
With the words of line 96: "Love justice, you who judge the earth." It is the opening verse of the Book of Wisdom, which was read as King Solomon's advice to rulers.
Diligite, "love", is the verb. Justitiam, "justice", is the noun.

quote: the M of the fifth word
note: The last letter of TERRAM, "earth". Many readers take the M to stand for monarchy, the single world empire that Dante believed God intended. The rounded M of medieval lettering is also a shape that can grow into a bird.
The planet is silver white. The souls are golden lights set in it.

quote: sparks that fools read as omens
note: A country custom: people struck a burning log and counted the sparks, hoping for as many coins or lambs.

quote: the head and neck of an eagle
context: The figure forms in three steps. The souls make an M, more lights settle on its top, and the letter becomes the outline of an eagle.

note: God, the artist of this picture, who works from no model.

quote: that power which shapes the nest
note: A hard line. It is usually read to mean that the instinct by which every bird builds its nest comes from God, as does all the forming power in nature.

quote: bloom like lilies on the M
note: For this Dante coins a verb, ingigliarsi, "to enlily itself". With the extra lights on top, the M looks for a moment like a heraldic lily, the emblem of the French kings and of Guelph Florence. Then it becomes the eagle of the empire. Many readers see a political point in the change.

quote: that heaven you adorn with light
note: Each planet was thought to shed its own influence on the earth. Jupiter's is justice.
The papal court. Its greed is the smoke that dims the planet's rays, so that justice fails on earth.

quote: the buying and selling in the temple
note: In the Gospels, Christ drove the merchants and money changers out of the Temple in Jerusalem with a whip. The Church, built on the blood of the martyrs, has become a market again.
Excommunication and interdict, which cut people or whole cities off from the Mass and the sacraments. The popes of Dante's time used them as weapons of politics and war.

quote: you who write only to cross out
note: Most commentators see Pope John XXII, who reigned from 1316 to 1334, while Dante was writing the Paradiso. The charge is that he issued excommunications in order to be paid to cancel them.
The two apostles, both put to death in Rome by tradition. The vineyard is the Church, a figure from the Gospels.

quote: him who chose to live as a hermit
note: John the Baptist, who lived in the desert and was beheaded as a reward for Salome's dancing. His figure was stamped on the florin, the gold coin of Florence. The pope's devotion is to the coin, not the saint.
Saint Peter, a fisherman before he followed Christ, and by tradition the first pope. The pope is made to speak of his own founder as a stranger.
